name: Interslavic zonal constructed language
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.source_named: Jan van Steenbergen, Interslavic pronunciation page, steen.free.fr/interslavic/read 2026-08-31)
earlier_scan.note: Free stress by design; recommended guidelines favor initial/near-initial stress, stress unaffected by inflection.

new_statements.quote: Stress is on the first syllable of short words. That syllable is only slightly emphasized, just like in the English words "table", "memory". Long words have the stress on the internal syllable where there are more consonants - just like in the English word "December". However, Interslavic is an artificial language and therefore allows different kinds of stress. Polish speakers, for example, will tend to put the stress on the second to last syllable of a word; Czechs will tend to put stress always on the first syllable of a word.
new_statements.citation: Merunka, Vojtěch. 2018. Interslavic zonal constructed language: an introduction for English-speakers. Prague: Slovanská unie z. s. (print ISBN 978-80-907004-9-9; e-ISBN 978-80-904932-7-8), 166 pp. Chapter 1 'pronunciation and alphabet', section 'pronunciation'.
new_statements.locator: p. 33 (PDF page 25 of the CEEOL Sample-PDF, id 808239)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (41-page CEEOL Sample-PDF, text layer present, no scanned needed). PDF page 25 carries printed page number 33 under the heading "1. pronunciation and alphabet / pronunciation"; the TOC PDF confirms ch. 1 "pronunciation and alphabet" and "pronunciation" both at p. 33. The passage is there verbatim: "Stress is on the first syllable of short words. That syllable is only slightly emphasized, just like in the English words "table", "memory". Long words have the stress on the internal syllable where there are more consonants - just like in the English word "De-/cember". However, Interslavic is an artificial language and therefore allows different kinds of stress. Polish speakers, for examp…
new_statements.rule_in_words: By design there is no fixed word-stress rule: stress is free and speaker-dependent (each Slavic accent is 'equally correct'). The recommended default (Merunka 2018) is initial stress in short words and stress on an internal, consonant-heavy syllable in longer words; the co-designer's grammar (van Steenbergen, steen.free.fr) states 'Accentuation is free' and recommends first syllable in 2-syllable words, first/second in 3-syllable, second/third in 4-syllable words, with stress not shifting under inflection and kept off prefixes, suffixes and endings. No fixed-list category matches 'free/variable by design'; the closest defensible label would otherwise be a recommended (not obligatory) initial/near-initial default.
new_statements.exceptions: Speaker-dependent variation is explicitly allowed (Polish speakers penultimate, Czech speakers initial). van Steenbergen adds: stress should not be influenced by inflection (běly → bělogo with the same stressed syllable) and should avoid prefixes, suffixes and case endings.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; prescriptive recommendation for an artificial auxiliary language with no native speakers, not a description of usage. Merunka's 'short'/'long' word threshold is not defined. van Steenbergen's page also notes that Russian-style akanje (reduction of unstressed vowels) should be avoided.
new_statements.identity_note: Interslavic (isv, glottocode inte1263) is a constructed zonal auxiliary language with no native speakers; both quoted sources describe the unified 2017 standard (merger of Slovianski and Neoslavonic) — Merunka 2018 is by one co-designer, steen.free.fr by the other (Jan van Steenbergen). Merunka 2012 in the list of works to obtain describes the predecessor Neoslavonic (no separate glottocode known to me). Stress statements are prescriptive recommendations, not observations of a speech community.

new_statements.quote: Ударение в межславянском языке свободное. Однако, если вы хотите оставаться на безопасной стороне, рекомендуется следовать некоторым рекомендациям. [description] Когда в слове 2 слога ударение падает на первый слог. Когда в слове 3 слога ударение падает на первый или второй слог. Когда в слове 4 слога ударение падает на второй или третий слог. По факту, эти три правила можно свести к одному. Ударение падает на второй или третий слог с конца. [...] Слово изменение не должно влиять на ударение. [...] В целом, лучше избегать ударения, падающего на приставки, суффиксы, падежные окончания и так далее. [ASR 1:26-2:14]
new_statements.translation: Stress in Interslavic is free. However, if you want to stay on the safe side, it is recommended to follow certain recommendations. [description] When a word has 2 syllables, stress falls on the first syllable. When a word has 3 syllables, stress falls on the first or second syllable. When a word has 4 syllables, stress falls on the second or third syllable. In fact these three rules can be reduced to one: stress falls on the second or third syllable from the end. [...] Inflection must not affect the stress. [...] In general it is better to avoid stress falling on prefixes, suffixes, case endings and so on.
new_statements.citation: Ranmaru Rei. 2023. 'Урок 2: Ударение в межславянском языке' [Lesson 2: Stress in Interslavic], video lesson (archive.org mirror youtube-f8GMCU_NgNI).
new_statements.locator: Whole video (4 min 01 s) is about stress. Written description (0:00 card); spoken rule 1:16-2:14 (76-134 s); zákaz/zamok remarks 2:14-2:40; imperative exception 2:41-3:12 with a conjugation table on screen at 3:09; closing remarks 3:13-3:40. On-screen slide at 1:40 shows the same three-line rule in Russian.
new_statements.relation_note: Not in the catalog; one existing statement (Merunka 2018, p. 33, read as 'unclear or contradictory': short words initial, long words on the internal syllable with more consonants). The video restates the official steen.free.fr 'Stress (Naglas)' section (same wording as the saved : 'Accentuation is free.. two syllables: first; three: first or second; four: second or third; stress should not be influenced by inflection.. avoid stress on prefixes, suffixes, case endings'), so it agrees with Merunka on free/loose stress and initial stress in short words, but formulates the long-word guideline by syllable count from the end (penult/antepenult window, paradigm-uniform, off affixes) rather than by…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free (not fixed; each speaker may stress as in their native Slavic language, the presenter names Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Bulgarian and Serbo-Croatian as comparable free-stress languages). The recommended 'safe' placement is a penult-or-antepenult window: disyllables initial; trisyllables 1st or 2nd; four-syllable words 2nd or 3rd, which the presenter sums up as 'second or third syllable from the end'. Stress stays on the same syllable throughout the paradigm (bě́ly, gen. bě́logo not bělógo) and should avoid prefixes, suffixes and case endings. The presenter notes the guidelines leave zákaz vs zakáz undecided (he prefers the latter) and that zámok/zamók are pronounced alike.
new_statements.exceptions: One exception the presenter adds (2:41-3:12): in the imperative of second-conjugation verbs the stress is recommended on the ending to distinguish it from the present tense: present dári, dárim, dárite vs imperative darí, darím, daríte (table 'Dariti' shown on screen at 3:09). He also notes that the guidelines do not settle zákaz vs zakáz (prefix vs final syllable) and that zamok 'castle' and zamok 'lock' end up homophonous; closing remark that speakers may simply use the stress they are used to (Polish penult, Czech/Slovak initial, Serbo-Croatian never final).
new_statements.identity_note: The video describes standard Interslavic (Medžuslovjansky) as codified on the official site steen.free.fr/interslavic (van Steenbergen), which it opens on screen and paraphrases in Russian; it is a learner's lesson by a Russian-speaking YouTuber (channel @RanmaruRei), not a linguistic description, and the imperative-stress exception is the presenter's own recommendation.

readall_conflicts: No hard conflict: every source opened (this video; the steen.free.fr pronunciation page it reads from, already held by the project; Merunka 2018 p. 33 in existing_statements) treats Interslavic stress as free/non-fixed with only recommendations. The recommendations differ in formulation: van Steenbergen's site and the video give a penult-or-antepenult window by syllable count, paradigm-uniform and off affixes; Merunka 2018 gives initial stress for short words and, for long words, the internal syllable 'where there are more consonants'. These are different heuristics, not contradictory fixed rules. The video's imperative-ending exception (darí, darím, daríte) is the presenter's own addition ('one small exception'), not found in the saved steen pronunciation page or the Merunka sample PDF.
